name: Mathspace
line: Mathspace checks each line of work for a teacher's class. AMP picks every problem and counts only unaided answers.
description: AMP vs Mathspace: Mathspace checks each line of working for school classes. AMP picks every problem, counts only unaided answers and schedules review.
verdict: Mathspace checks every line of a student's working, is free for any single student, and costs schools $8 or $15 a student a year [2][1]. It is built around tasks a teacher assigns, and its adaptive tasks award diamonds for answers given after hints [4]. AMP chooses every problem itself, counts only answers given without help toward mastery, brings learned skills back on a schedule, and runs from counting to precalculus.

reasons.title: Mastery means right without help
reasons.body: In an adaptive task, Mathspace awards diamonds for a correct final answer "no matter if" the student used hints, videos or lessons; only the Next Step button withholds them [4]. Its adaptive tasks now end after a set amount of practice, 6 to 15 stars over three rounds, not when the student reaches mastery [5]. In AMP a skill shows as Strong only when four of the last five answers are right without help, and an answer after a hint or the lesson does not move the level. A record built that way shows what the learner can do alone.

reasons.title: AMP chooses every next problem
reasons.body: In Mathspace a teacher assigns tasks [6]. After check-ins, the dashboard recommends tasks, and the student can shuffle them or change the Skills Focus that drives them [7][8]. Inside an adaptive task, questions start easier and get harder as the student shows understanding [6]. AMP keeps a level in each of 14 strands of math and chooses each next problem from the learner's answers: new work just within reach, a prerequisite, or review. Nobody has to build a task first.

reasons.title: Misses lead back to the missing piece
reasons.body: Mathspace lists a topic's missing prerequisite skills as gaps, and recommends a topic as ready only once its prerequisites are mastered [9][7]. In the help articles we read, it does not send a struggling student back to a prerequisite on its own; the readiness article leaves the choice to the student and suggests teachers set a date for filling gaps [9]. In AMP two misses in a row on a skill send practice to what that skill builds on. No one has to notice first.

reasons.title: Learned skills come back on a schedule
reasons.body: Mathspace's Revision bank holds questions a student has not yet answered correctly. A missed question returns after some time, with no interval given, and one correct answer removes it for good [10]. We found no scheduled review of skills already mastered [10]. AMP brings each learned skill back after 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month, mixed with other topics, and a miss starts the schedule over.

reasons.title: Built for a family to run at home
reasons.body: Mathspace sells paid plans only to schools and other education institutions, with a minimum of 30 licences [1]. A family can use the free Personal account, but Mathspace says it does not offer a parent or guardian login. It offers parents emails instead: weekly summaries on its pricing page, and a reminder of tasks due the next day in its help center [1][12]. AMP is sold to families. The parent sees the level in every strand, the skills, the time and the actual problems, and has nothing to assign.

reasons.title: From counting to precalculus, at any pace
reasons.body: In the US, Mathspace maps its content to standards for grades 3 to 12 [13], and Wikipedia describes its US range as grade 3 to Algebra 2 [18]. A student's grade level is set from their class unless a teacher overrides it, and recommended tasks run from grade 3 up to that grade [15]. AMP runs from counting through precalculus on one map of 336 skills. While a learner is climbing, every second problem reaches higher, and a parent can open any skill directly.

reasons.title: Printed workbooks made for one learner
reasons.body: Mathspace prints worksheets for select textbooks, and teachers can build class worksheets with answer keys in a beta [16][17]. We found nothing that prints a different workbook for each student from that student's own work. AMP prints unlimited workbooks composed from each learner's record, each with a worked answer key, and results entered from paper count toward the level.

rows.price: Free Personal account for one class of up to 30. Schools: $8 (Classes) or $15 (Schools) per student per year. Schools Plus and districts by quote [1].
rows.buyers: Schools and other education institutions, minimum 30 licences [1]. Any student or teacher can open a free Personal account. No parent login [1].
rows.range: Content mapped to standards for grades 3 to 12 in the US [13]; Wikipedia gives grade 3 to Algebra 2 [18]. Nothing below grade 3.
rows.start: Skills Check-ins: an adaptive test on a Bayesian IRT model, reported as a grade level such as 8.5 [23]. The grade level is set from the student's class [15].
rows.teaching: Textbook lessons with videos, step-by-step hints, a worked solution for every textbook question, and Milo, an AI chat tutor [19][20][24][14].
rows.next: Teacher-assigned tasks, plus recommended topics the student chooses among. Inside a task, questions get harder as mastery rises [6][7].
rows.mastery: A target of Proficient or Mastered; we found no published thresholds [6][36]. Tasks end after 6 to 15 stars [5]; diamonds count answers given after hints [4].
rows.review: Revision: missed questions return after an unstated time and leave after one correct answer. No scheduled review of mastered skills found [10].
rows.print: Printable worksheets for select textbooks, answer keys, and custom class worksheets in beta [16][1][17]. We found none made from one student's record.
rows.adult: A teacher builds and assigns tasks with due dates, sets target mastery, and reads reports [6][22][35]. On a free account the learner largely directs themselves [1][11].
rows.reports: Task, student and class reports, a live view and an administrator dashboard [1]. Parents get emails, not a login: weekly summaries and due-task reminders [1][12].
rows.evidence: One Utah state evaluation comparing users with non-users: positive only for students using it over 33 minutes a week [29]. Evidence for ESSA: no rating [31].

theirs: Mathspace is made by Mathspace Pty Ltd of Sydney, Australia, founded in 2010 [18][25]. It is an online math program for schools: an interactive textbook, practice that checks each line of working, adaptive tasks, diagnostic check-ins and an AI chat tutor called Milo [19][14]. US content is mapped to standards in every state for grades 3 to 12 [13], and districts can adopt it as a core curriculum, Mathspace Core [19]. Its Parents page counts 725,671 students worldwide [11].

Work comes from three places: tasks a teacher assigns, practice recommended after check-ins, and a Revision bank of missed questions [6][7][10]. Inside a question, the student writes the solution line by line, typed on the web or handwritten on an iPad, and each line is marked as it is entered [20][21][2]. Hints, for some questions a video of a similar problem, the lesson, a calculator, Milo and a Next Step button sit beside the work [20][14]. An adaptive task runs three rounds, and afterwards Fix mode lets the student redo missed questions until the due date [5][22].
Paid plans are for schools and other education institutions [1]. A family can use the free Personal account, with no parent login and no paid family plan [1].
credit: It checks the student's own working, line by line. Each step is judged as it is entered, valid methods the authors did not foresee are accepted, and steps on a recommended path get hints made for that step [2][3]. AMP checks typed lines of work on 64 problem types; it does not check freehand working step by step.
Price. Any student or teacher can use a Personal account free, and schools pay $8 or $15 per student per year [1]. AMP costs far more per student.

Far more video and content: over 14,000 instructional videos, 40,000 question templates, and a worked solution for every textbook question [19][24]. AMP's films cover a growing share of problem types, far fewer than that.
Things AMP does not have: an iPad app with handwriting, an AI chat tutor that teachers can read and switch off, read-aloud in beta, and points, streaks and avatars in beta [25][21][14][26][27].
Outside review: EdReports rated its high school series as meeting expectations for focus, coherence and rigor, and as partially meeting expectations for usability [28]. AMP has no EdReports review.

theirs: The outcome evidence we found is one state evaluation. The Utah Education Policy Center at the University of Utah studied the 2018-19 school year of the Utah STEM Action Center's grant program, through which schools bought licenses with state grant funds [29]. It compared 2,105 Mathspace users with 11,319 students from propensity-matched schools that did not use the funded programs, adjusting for student characteristics [29]. Users were compared with non-users; it was not a randomized trial.

Results depended on use. Only students using Mathspace more than 33 minutes a week differed significantly: a 9% higher probability of proficiency on Utah's RISE test (odds ratio 1.45) and growth percentiles 3.92 points higher. The two middle usage groups showed no significant difference, and students using it under 6 minutes a week had growth percentiles 4.67 points lower. Half the users logged 12 minutes a week or less [29]. Students who use a program most can differ from the rest before they start, so the study cannot show that Mathspace caused the gain.

Mathspace's Parents page cites a study of 94,000 students and a 53% increase in the likelihood of proficiency [11]. The company's blog places that study in Utah's 2017-18 school year, says 6,588 of those students used Mathspace, and does not state the design or give effect sizes [30]. Evidence for ESSA lists Mathspace without a rating: "No studies met inclusion requirements" [31]. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report for it as of November 2026 [32]. EdReports rates alignment and usability, not learning outcomes [28].
ours: Where AMP and Mathspace part ways, we built AMP on methods with strong research behind them. A review of ten common study techniques rated two as high utility: practice testing and spaced practice [33]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [34]. AMP schedules that review for every learned skill, and counts only answers given without help, so its record shows what a learner can do alone. We expect that to show in outcomes. That is our bet, and we have committed in public to measuring it.

AMP is new, and its own outcome studies have not run yet. They begin in 2027: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. Until then, the research behind each part of AMP is laid out in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want each line of a student's written working checked, typed or handwritten on an iPad [2][21].
You need it free: any student can open a Personal account [1].
You run a school that wants a low per-student price, teacher-assigned tasks, and a high school series EdReports has reviewed [1][28].
You want an AI chat tutor, or read-aloud (in beta), built in [14][26].
amp: You are a family and want a program sold to you, with your own view of every skill and every problem.
Your child is below grade 3, or you want one program from counting through precalculus.
You want mastery to mean right without help.
You want old skills to come back on a schedule, and misses to lead back to the missing piece, without anyone planning it.
You want printed workbooks made for one learner, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: Can parents buy Mathspace?
questions.answer: Not as a paid plan. Mathspace sells paid packages only to schools and other education institutions, with a minimum of 30 licences, and says it does not offer a parent or guardian login [1]. A student can use the free Personal account. AMP is sold directly to families, and the parent sees everything.

questions.question: Is AMP more expensive than Mathspace?
questions.answer: Yes. Mathspace is free for a single student, and schools pay $8 or $15 per student per year [1]. AMP costs a family $599 a year or $59 a month for the first child, then $399 or $39 for each more. That covers counting through precalculus, unlimited personalized workbooks, and two parents' own practice, and the first 100 answers and 5 workbooks are free.

questions.question: Does AMP check every step like Mathspace?
questions.answer: No. Mathspace marks each line of working and accepts any valid method [2][3]. AMP checks final answers exactly, and typed lines of work on 64 problem types, then shows worked steps after every answer.

questions.question: My child uses Mathspace at school. Can we use AMP at home?
questions.answer: Yes. AMP is a separate program. It places the learner within the first 24 problems and keeps a level in each of 14 strands of math, then chooses practice and schedules review on its own.
